utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness for the Prosecution will be Mr. Robert Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As Your Honours are well aware, Mr. Donia's report was admitted pursuant to Your Honour's decision earlier last month; however very recently we filed a small corrigenda, which Mr. Donia prepared to that report. Accordingly, what I propose to do is circulate for everyone's ease a copy of that report and ask Mr. Donia a couple of very short questions relating to the report and core agenda, ask for an exhibit number to be put on the report, and ask for the corrigenda to be admitted as well. If you distribute those copies, please. If everybody has the copies, then I'll begin

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, could you please state your full name and date of birth for the record?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Robert J. Donia; I was born May 30th, 1945.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And were you asked to prepare an expert report for use in this case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you see that report on the lectern in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Donia doesn't have copy of his corrigenda. Could he please be given this as well. And for Mr. Registrar, the e-court number of the report is 02963.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And beside you as well on the lectern now, do you see a copy of the corrigenda that you prepared and we filed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that bears the 65 ter 03045. I would ask, Your Honour, now that pursuant to the decision that a number be assigned to Mr. Donia's report, and the corrigenda to the report be admitted as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 02963 will be admitted as P472, and the corrigenda 03045 will be admitted as P473.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. That being done, the report and corrigenda being admitted Your Honour, the Prosecution will not be asking any further questions of Dr. Donia and produces him for cross-examination by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Tapuskovic. Mr. Tapuskovic, it's your turn to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me just collect my material. I was except expecting the Prosecutor to use her one hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps while Mr. Tapuskovic collects his material, I have made an error in the ter number I have given to the corrigenda. It actually bears the ter number 0344 -- 03044. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Evidently you have taken Mr. Tapuskovic by surprise, Ms. Edgerton, but I don't know why. It's a Rule 94 procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is not the fact that I did not have my material ready. I was merely preparing to hear the examination-in-chief; however, I am ready to examine Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I'm the Defence counsel for Dragomir Milosevic. Several years ago we met briefly whilst I was amicus curiae, and I examined you in that capacity for a short period of time. On this occasion, however, I will have some more time at my disposal to go through the topics contained in your paper. As far as I was able to see in this extensive report, there are as many as 74 paragraphs. I did my best to focus only on the parts I consider significant for the defence of Dragomir Milosevic. Out of the 74 topics, I will be -- or rather, paragraphs, I will be focussing on some 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm told by my colleague that none of the material that I wanted to base my examination on can you found in e-court. I'm told that the material will be there soon. I had to mark my papers with reference to the paragraphs to facilitate my examination of the expert witness. It's not in e-court yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that the technician is addressing, or will shortly be addressing, that problem. Well, can you start with something else that doesn't require e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid not, but we have it now, it seems. This is Prosecution Exhibit P362, and I cross-referenced it with paragraphs. My copy of the report, as well as the English version, has paragraphs marked on it, and can we please have the English version retrieved so that Your Honours can follow my cross-examination. That's the same document I was referring to. I only want the version that I uploaded into e-court because I was forced to work with some paragraphs to make my cross-examination easier. I'm not sure if that's what we have on our screens now. Very well. Now I can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, let us first look at introduction, which can be found on page 4 in both versions. You state there that you made this report as a historical background and political and military context for events alleged in the indictment in the ICTY case, case number IT-98-29/1-T, The Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that the report focussed on the events, on developments from November 1990, when multi-party elections brought nationalists to power, to August 1994. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, then, that the situation existing on the ground between August 1994 and November 1995, as well as the political and military circumstances, are something that you did not take into consideration at all. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I wouldn't say I didn't take them into consideration at all, because I had to have some understanding of them to prepare the background report, but I have not addressed those in the report, I think, except for one sentence toward the end in which I discussed the period until the actual negotiations that led to peace in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we take it that, for instance, you did not consider the following fact at all; namely, that in early August 1994, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia employed a sanction-type approach toward the JNA. You did not take this into account at all. I only found one sentence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I did not address the issue of whether or not there was a sanction regime -- sanctions regime, in effect in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also go on to say in the introduction that multi-party elections brought nationalities to power. Was this true for all the sides, for all the parties to these events? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: You mean within Bosnia-Herzegovina, if I can clarify your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since this opinion concerns the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I primarily had that in mind, yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, you say that this report of yours dealt with all these matters based on materials from the research library of the University of Michigan, your own personal library, documents made available by the Office of the Prosecutor. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: By your profession, you're primarily a historian, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to problems concerns linguistics and language and constitutional and legal matters, you do not have any expertise, do you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next page, the first paragraph on that page, and the heading: "Peoples and Nationalism, Sarajevo, and the Multi-party Elections of 1990." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the first sentence, you speak of Communism collapsing in eastern Europe and of multi-party elections being held throughout the region?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say the following: "In the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, SFRY, country-wide elections were never called." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that back at that time, or rather, from 1945 up to 1990, there was a system in place that was imposed by the communist authority of Josip Broz Tito?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that all the structures of power were controlled by people who were members of the communist party, and there were roughly around two million of them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: League of Communists is the term; but in large measures, yes, there were, particularly in the later years of socialism, more and more people of influence who were not party members. But as a generalisation, I would agree with your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, some two million people decided the fate of some 22 million people. That was the population of Yugoslavia and, of course, we're talking in rough terms. Can you confirm this for me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I qualify that by saying more and more people had more control other than own destinies, and more non-party members played important roles in various institutions, particularly of institutions of self-management in the latter years of socialism in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, in all those years, especially up until 1960, all those who were of dissenting opinions and expressed different opinions were imprisoned. You are familiar with the inform bureau period, the Goli Otok facility, and -- and 90 per cent of the cases involved Serbs and Montenegrins. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. Your premise is not correct, not everyone was imprisoned, and the people who were the subject of repression or prosecution were of various groups within Yugoslavia. I would think, for example, if one looked at the year 1971, would be completely the opposite for the number of people who were punished or imprisoned. So, no, I would say -- I would reject your premise there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was yet to come to 1971. That's why I deliberately emphasised the period between 1948 and 1960 as well as Goli Otok. And, at that time, they were imprisoned because some people favoured the Soviet Union. That was the inform bureau case, and many of them were imprisoned back in the Adriatic Sea.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I would, nonetheless, reject your premise or your assertion. There was a period of time between about 1949 and 1952 when the majority of political repression was directed against conformists. Their nationalities, again, were various. I don't know of any reliable statistic that would say that 90 per cent of them were Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Up until 1952, they were put in prison, but they stayed there until 1960 without any judicial decision being passed. Did you know that they were basically kept for as many as 20 years in very harsh circumstances in these prisons, simply pursuant to administrative decisions. Are you an aware of this or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: You're making a very broad generalisation that I could not accept, could not agree with you on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying. None of the material that speaks extensively of these events is familiar to you. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm familiar with certainly some works and studies of that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The events you mentioned concerning 1972 had to do primarily with constitutional change. All those who were opposed to the amendments to the constitution in 1974, most of them law professor, did you know that several of them were arrested and many more kicked out of the university because their version of the constitution did not fit where the general situation at the time? Let's put it that way. Those were judicial decisions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Your question pertained to 1971, I believe, which is a period when the so-called Croatian Spring flourished and hundreds of Croats were arrested and many purged from the party, and that would certainly be one of the largest episodes of political repression, not only at that time, but throughout the socialist period. You then asked a question about 1974 and the constitution, and, yes, it's true that there were a few people arrested and imprisoned for views that were construed as anti-state at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you mentioned 1971 Croatian Spring, was that an attempt by Croatia to secede from Yugoslavia as earlier as then in a forcible way? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to your report. You say that the SFRY never had country-wide elections, or rather, they were never called as was normally done throughout the world. Do you know that more than half of the SFRY population was Serbs living in Serbia, Croatian, Lika, Kordun, Dalmatia from the beginning of time in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Montenegro, and there were some present also in there Slovenia and Macedonia? Is not a notorious fact that there were more than ten million Serbs living not only in Serbia but in all the other parts of the country that had lived as one for almost 70 years?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, out of 22 million, half of them were not Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I believe the census figures showed that of the Yugoslav population about 34, 35 per cent identified themselves as Serbs by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You should have the basis for this statement that you make. You should be referring to an underlying document. If you can refer me to a single document supporting this, I will withdraw my question. Is it true that seven million people living in Serbia were ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't recall the census data on the number of Serbs either in Serbia proper or in the SFRJ in the 1981 or 1991 census, but certainly a very knowable number. The percentage of Serbs in Yugoslavia was nowhere near the 50 per cent that you suggested in your initial question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it right that roughly 1.5 million Serbs lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I believe I gave you that number in the appendix to my report, and that is approximately correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct between 600 and 700 thousand Serbs living in Croatia, I believe this is stated in your report, 600.000 or 12 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the time only Serbs lived in Montenegro, though with a small fraction of Albanians and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, part of that population of Montenegro considered themselves Montenegrin and part considered themselves Serbs to my understanding. So I would say no to the premise of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were probably reading newspapers recently, because that's the opinion that has prevailed now every since Montenegro have is seceded from Serbia. I was talking about the 1990s, and the escalation of the crisis at the time. In that period, weren't the Serbs living in Montenegro primarily Serbs, but considered themselves to be Montenegrin as well, since they lived in that general area. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: So you're saying that they were Serbs and Montenegrins at the same time? Is your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us not belabour the point. It's quite a sensitive matter. Let me go directly to what I have been meaning to ask you. Had democratic elections been organised ever in Yugoslavia and had the peoples living in Yugoslavia in 1990 there, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims - and this is somewhere in your report - especially Bosnian Muslims, who appreciated the fact that they were part of Yugoslavia. Isn't that right? You wrote that in your report that the Muslims were highly appreciative of the fact that they lived in Yugoslavia. I will refer you to the specific part of your report later on.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, had it been fob for democratic elections to be organised in 1990, given the general situation and the sentiments of the people, would those people ever have decided to go their separate ways, or would they have opted for a common life had these democratic election that Josip Broz had been preventing from happening for 50 years, in fact, been organized?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In 1990, the non-Serb peoples of Yugoslavia, and even many of the Serbs, had become very fearful of Serbian hegemony, as it was being manifested in the Milosevic regime. So it's hard for me to imagine that the country-wide election would have resulted in a harmonious vote in favour of Yugoslavia. I have to say in any case it would be speculation as to how those elections might have come out. They were certainly opposed by the Republic of Serbia and Milosevic, as well as the Slovene leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We will there, sir. Let's forget Milosevic for a moment. If the people who lived in that country had been asked, do you think that they would have opted for war if a referendum had been called or would they have opted for the continuation of the peaceful life that they had for 50 years in a region in which there was no long stretch of peace of 50 years at anytime before in that history. What do you think they would have opted for, including the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know any country in which people would vote for war over peace, and I think it's rather an absurd proposition to suggest that such a election would ever be held. It certainly wasn't held in Yugoslavia, anywhere in Yugoslavia in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly why I am asking. Slobodan Milosevic is one problem, but what was worrying the Croats and the Slovenians is that they were aware that if all the people had been asked, the country would have -- wouldn't have fallen apart. It would have stayed a whole. Milosevic is another topic. So for the first time in their history, they would have had to -- they would have had their say in democratic elections. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, as I think your question implies, you can't forget Milosevic and the impact that his actions had on general attitudes, which made the non-Serb peoples turn very much against continued participation in Yugoslavia at that time and accounts for, in large measure, the success of nationalist parties in the various elections, not only in Bosnia and Herzegovina but in the other republics that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one more question. We'll get there yet. But you mentioned 1984 also, and you also mention Milosevic's influence upon separatism and hegemonism, et cetera. But where was Milosevic in 1984? Slobodan Milosevic did not exist in 1984 when the constitution of 1984 was passed, but we will get there yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did Milosevic have to do with 1974? I will show you the place in your document where you mention him as the bearer of all the principles, counter to the interests of all other people. I would like a yes or no answer from you, but we'll get there. Where was Milosevic in 1974 and in 1971 at the time of Croatian Spring?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There may be a translation problem, but I think -- I never mentioned 1984, but did speak of 1974. And as far as I know, Slobodan Milosevic was a banker in Belgrade and member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take this up after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have an hour and a half, or an hour and 35 minutes, and the cross-examination should be concluded by that time, if not before that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a very lengthy document. I have shortened it to 20. I really had to be very strict in my selection. I will try, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Concentrate on the important issues. Some of the issues you have been dealing with thus far do not appear to the Chamber to be so vital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if there had been democracy in communist Yugoslavia, there would have been no war and we would have been living peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you a little while ago about 1974, not 1984. At the time when the constitution was fashioned in 1974, Josip Broz Tito was still alive. He was 82 years of age. Is that so? Do you know that this was a kind of concession to the Croatian Spring in order to satisfy the appetites of Slovene and Croatia for them to achieve independence some day as easy as possible.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. I think it was an effort to provide, let's say, a legal and societal republic-level autonomy at the same time that the unity of the country should be guaranteed by the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it then that the veto principle was introduced. Is it correct that two autonomous provinces were created that had attributes of statehood, and the were located in the territory of Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That was a couple of different questions. It was the time at which a veto principle was introduced in the federal legislative bodies. The two autonomous provinces had existed under those names since 1945 and were given additional authority or an increased role both in the Federation and increased autonomy under the terms of the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that throughout that history, the period of Tito, there were attempts to give the Serbs in Krajina the same kind of autonomy that was granted to Kosovo and Vojvodina in Serbia. Are you familiar with that from numerous documents and a great amount of literature?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There were -- yes. There were ideas of such floated at various times by people, along with ideas for autonomy of other peoples and groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say at any rate that by the introduction of the veto right, the right that was granted to the provinces, too, the Republic of Serbia became unable to take any decision in the interest of the people, because every time there would -- an important decision, a vital decision in the interest of the people was tried to be passed, it would be vetoed. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then let us take a look at what you are saying here. At first elections were held in Croatia and Slovenia. Is it right that the Slovenian and Croatian constitutions were changed before that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the Serbs, who lived in Slovenia, there was a substantial number of them in Slovenia; and the Serbs in Croatia who had the status of constitutive people, did they lose that status under the terms of the new constitution and became a minority? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: For Slovenia, I don't know. The number of Serbs was really quite small in Slovenia. As far as Croatia, did the Serb lose their status as a constituent nation, yes, they did, in the constitution of May or June of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the right to their language.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Not completely, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. But since we're dealing with Bosnia-Herzegovina here, you know that that part of former SFRJ, or rather, that republic was a very specific because three peoples lived there; Muslims, Serbs and Croats. The share of the Croats and the Bosnian population was below that of the Serbs in Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I think there's two questions in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Questions one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think I can answer them. The first question was: Did three constituent peoples live in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the answer is yes; Serbs, Croats, and Bosnian Muslims, and there were additional small groups or -- small other groups that lived there. And the second part of your question was whether the -- I think the per cent of Serbs in -- the per cent of Serbs in Croatia was about 12 per cent. The per cent of Croats in Bosnia was about 17 per cent, according to the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. My question is the following: About the abolishment of the constituent quality to any one of these peoples ensue in serious tension, let us not go as far as conflict? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not quite sure I understand the question. Would you kindly pose it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that republic, three peoples lived which was not the case in any other republic. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If any of these three peoples had lost the right to decide together with the others, in other words, if they had lost the status of constituent nation, would that result in serious tensions? Was that easy to foresee?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, not particularly. The three nations kept their constituent status through March of 1994, and clearly there were many tensions and conflict -- conflicts that occurred prior to that time. So saying that the loss of constituent status at the constitutional level would generate tensions or conflict would be kind of speculation for Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's clear that it did do that in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Didn't the dominant or position of one people and the outvoting of the other ensue in a civil war there, so that even the United Nations had to intervene?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The term "majarosaci" [phoen] or "majoritisation" was a term used by members of all three nations to characterise majority rule, and it was sort of brought into disrepute by the denunciations of particularly Serb and Croat nationalists. So I don't know that the process as much as the -- the process of majority rule as much as the rejection of majority rule by both Serbs and Croats -- Croat nationalists was the source of that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can accelerate a little, and we proceed to the second paragraph of your document. Can you tell me about the people who lived -- that lived in that country, the problem -- the issue of language, whatever you call it, Serbian and Croatian, Bosnian and Montenegrin, or whatever, was there ever a problem of communication? Did they have a problem in understanding each other during those 70 years? Was language ever a problem?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Language was a problem only for politicians who were power-hungry and acted in their interests as well as some theoreticians. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in your opinion you state that Croat, Serbs, and Bosnian Muslims of BiH all originated in migrations of Slavs to south-eastern Europe in the fifth through eighth centuries A.D. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me where you're saying in the fifth through eight centuries, at that time, Slavic tribes of which the most numerous were the Serbs and Croats settled in the Balkans. At that time there could have been no Bosnian nation; is that so? They couldn't have called themselves Bosnian while they were still living in the Carpathians?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: We had no evidence that they did. The origin of the name "Bosnian" is not completely certain, so I suppose it's possible that they may have carried that -- a tribe may have carried that name with it. But that is really something about which we know very little or nothing for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But much is known about that. There are international and Yugoslav authoritative texts about that, that some Slavic tribes inhabited certain areas of the Balkans. They were mostly Croatians and Serbian tribes, and they had arrived in the Balkans. And let me refer to something else. You say in your second sentence that they spoke Bosnian, Croatian, Serbian, abbreviated B/C/S. How could they have spoken Bosnian when they arrived to Bosnia as Slavs? Can you provide a logical explanation at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think there is a considerable consensus among scholars that the migration of what became the south Slavs was -- probably took place by tribes, and that the names of two of those tribes were Serbs and Croats. As I say, there is considerable agreement on that, although nationalists scholars of both Serbs and Croats would not share that view. The language that they spoke has undergone a number of changes in names and is referred to by differ peoples as -- under different names. The name of the language or languages that we use in this Tribunal is B/C/S, and I've -- since I am really not an expert in linguistics, but more of a consumer of that literature than a provider of it, I have used a formulation from a very recent book by two linguists and described the language as both one and three at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are referring to Ronel Alexander. Were there no better experts to rely on concerning the issue of languages.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you yourself said you are not an expert in linguistics, let us not dwell on this any longer. You went on to describe how the identity of those people living there was established, and towards the end you said that the most striking difference between them was religion; that is to say, Orthodox faith, Catholicism, or Islam. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Religious tradition was a key element of distinguishing these peoples one from the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now move to paragraph 4. That's page 6 in the English version, paragraph 3. Here you talk about how Sarajevo dates before Roman times. What is the significance of this settlement, which got this name only later, dates from pre-Roman times. What is the significance of that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand what your question is? The pre-Roman -- the significance of the pre-Roman settlement or the significance of Sarajevo? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since in the indictment it is said that Sarajevo was established before Christ, and here you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, if you continue along these lines, there is no way that I will entertain any submission from you to go beyond 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best to conclude my examination by 5.00 and to avoid staying a minute after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When we spoke a while ago about the faith that determined the identity of those peoples, you say here that the urban centre of Sarajevo, in its present location, was developed primarily during the Ottoman Empire in the mid-1400s. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim faith could not have been adopted by anyone prior to the arrival of the Ottoman conquerors. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. There is substantial evidence of conversions to Islam in advance of the Ottoman arrival in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How was that possible, since it is a historical fact that they started their conquest of Europe through Serbia sometime between 1460 and 1600?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Prior to that time, there were a number of conversions to Islam amongst people in the area who had been exposed to either the Islamic faith or had come to know it through travelling in Ottoman lands, and so there was probably a small number -- there were a small number of Muslims in Central Bosnia at about the time that the Ottomans actually conquered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give me any name of any scholar or authority or any source of this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There's substantial literature on this, as you may imagine, but Nedim Filipovic has written on this. Hasan Sabanovic, among others, have addressed that question of Islamisation and noted that aspect of the pre-Ottoman -- small number of pre-Ottoman conversions to Islam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of what ethnicity are these two authors that you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess they were -- certainly Hasan Sabanovic was a Bosnian Muslim. Nedim Filipovic, I believe, identified himself as a Yugoslav, but would either be Serb or Muslim as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to world renowned authorities. I was not referring to any member of the ethnic groups from that region. Therefore I was seeking a support for your thesis that it was possible for people to be converted to Islam prior to the arrival of the Ottoman conquerors?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is not an issue that has preoccupied, let's say, scholars of world history in any great numbers. I would say the best scholarship about it has been done by scholars in the late Yugoslav era, from about 1960 to 1985. So whatever their ethnicity, and I would say their ethnicity in this case is irrelevant, whatever their particular fame is in history, I view those studies as authoritative because they're well done, they're grounded on documentary evidence, and come from people who speak and read the languages necessary to interpret them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more thing in relation to this. Along with Islam, there were Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: At that time, and it's, what, 1460?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The vast majority of people in Central Bosnia in the area of Sarajevo, at that time, were either Catholics or members of the medieval Bosnian church, and there were some Orthodox as well. I think it's probably not appropriate to identify those people by ethnicity; that is, they were certainly Slavs and speakers of Slavic language. But for most purposes, they didn't identify themselves by ethnic identification as much as by religious affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My last question on this topic would be this: The Croat and Serb dominated Slavic tribes converted partly to Islam, some of the Croats but there were many more Serbs who adopted Islam as their faith?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, as I read the literature on conversions, most of conversions came from the Catholics -- most conversions to Islam came from Catholics and members of the Bosnian church, not Orthodoxy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were the ones who converted to Islam most, according to historical date. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. According to historians who studied this question, the vast majority came from Catholicism.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say the Croats were the ones -- the majority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, let's not say that, because most of them didn't identify themselves as Croats. They were Catholics or members of the Bosnian church, which was largely Catholic in there practice but independent of the Pope, and there's really not much to suggest that they thought of themselves or identified themselves as Croats. These were Slavic speakers whose primary identity was religious or with a religious tradition; in this case, Catholicism.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next sentence reads as follows, and I am very interested in hearing your explanation of this: "Sarajevo grew the most under different administrations: Ottoman, mainly 1460 to 1600; Austro-Hungarian, 1878 to 1980; and Communist Yugoslavia, 1945 to 1990." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about the period between 1878 [as interpreted] and 1990, you never mentioned in your report the events happening between 1914 and 1918; i.e., there is not a single mention of the First World War. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In the interest judicial economy, I have attempted to avoid a historical narrative, and instead focussed in this report on the primary historical actors that take part in the events of 1992 to 1995. So the purpose was not to provide any kind of historical narrative, and I make no representation that it is any way complete, but rather to identify the groups an individuals who played an important role.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, to follow on with that, I remind everybody that the title of Mr. Donia's report is "The Making of the Siege from 1990 to 1994," and I'm wondering about the relevance of this whole line of questioning at this stage of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's your response to that, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of my examination, I'm going to demonstrate the relevance of that. That's the whole point of this whole exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, Mr. Donia, there were more than 10 per cent of people living in Yugoslavia who lived through the two World Wars. Do you think that had any impact on the events that followed afterwards, in view of their experience from the First and Second World War? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely why I am asking you. How is it possible to talk about this siege, or siege in inverted comas, without first tackling the issue of the two World Wars. Do you know that in the First World War, Serbia, alongside with Montenegro, was on the side of the allied forces when Austro-Hungary attacked Serbia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that Austro-Hungarian army who entered Serbia were made up of Croats, Muslims, even Serbs who had been mobilised and were members of the Austrian army regiment; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it is a historical fact that can be found in all the encyclopedias around the world that around 40 per cent of Serbian men were killed during the First World War?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I can't confirm that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that the very few who survived were expelled from Serbia across Albania and that they had undergone a terrible ordeal in the process; is that true.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Serbian army withdrew, after being defeated, across Albania and regrouped on the island of Corfu. So I would say that they were driven out and force-marched themselves to the safer confines of Corfu. They were transported largely by the British from the land mass to the island of Corfu.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On their way, while crossing Albania, were they killed and did they die as a result of freezing. Is that also true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Many died of freezing, yes, and there was certainly some harassment of the retreating force on the part of Albanian irregulars at the time they were in march as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: They managed to get together in Thessaloniki in Greece and then joined the first ranks of Allied forces in order to continue the fight against the Austro-Hungarian units that were eventually expelled from Serbia. Is that also true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Treaty of Versailles, based on the will of Major Powers, was the basis for the kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes in spite of everything that Serbs had gone and suffered from these very same people. Is it true, then, that this state was created as a result of the will of superpowers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes was created on December 1, 1918 by fiat, or by order of the Serbian regent, Aleksander. The Versailles Treaty was not signed until sometime after that, so it makes no sense that the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes was a product of the Versailles Treaty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that Serbia could have expanded to include this entire area if it had not been from the will or the pressure from superpowers to create such a state and to incorporate the Croats and the Muslims from Austria and Hungary, who had previously crossed Serbia? So you're saying that this state was created against the will of the peoples?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think it was created with great enthusiasm and delight by the leaders of Serbia, the Kingdom of Serbia, and with the very willing participation of the political leaders of Croats and -- and Slovenes. Other peoples were opposed to it. The Albanian of Kosovo, for example, found this to be an imposition, a nationalists imposition and negation of their hopes to be part of an Albanian state. So I think some peoples -- or the leaders of some peoples joined enthusiastically in its creation, and others felt either that they were had been left out of the decision, which would be the case of the Bosnian Muslim, or were viewing that as a oppressive imposition, which would be the case of the Albanians of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Weren't the Kosovo Albanians on the side of Austro-Hungarian throughout the war and took part in many killings of Serbs. That's a historical fact?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I feel at this point I really have to renew my objection as to relevance to line of questioning. Mr. Tapuskovic did give an initial response when I raised the question the first time, but we have full circle and we're back to almost a 100 years before the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he did start with the Treaty of Versailles after the First World War, and I'm expecting you now to move to the Second World War because there a relationship between what happened. And I imagine he is going to establish that. So move to the Second World War now and deal with the Serb involvement in that war and, then move on quickly to the modern era.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was precisely my intention, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now we come to Second World War. Immediately and from the outset of the war, isn't it a fact that an independent Croatian state was established that was part of the Axis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Subsequent to the German invasion of Yugoslavia, the Germans and Italians agreed to set up a puppet state known as the Independent State of Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the first thing that -- what Hitler did in view of the uprising in Serbia was to raze Belgrade to the ground, and not only Belgrade but other towns in Serbia as well. The bombing started on the 6th of April, 1994, and thousands upon thousands of Serbs were killed in the process?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1941.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Germans bombed essentially all cities in the course of their invasion. Certainly, the heaviest bombardment in Belgrade and, yes the deaths from that ranged in the thousands. They also bombarded Sarajevo. Those casualties numbered in the many hundreds, and other cities as well. So the German attack on Yugoslavia was very costly in lives in a number of places, and the primary victims of that military assault it seems to me were indeed Serbs; the most numerous victims perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you say that Sarajevo was bombed. At the time, Sarajevo was part of the independent state of Croatia. Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of the banovina under the rule of NDH or the independent state of Croatia. Not a single bomb fell either on Sarajevo or Ljubljana. How can you account for that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: You have your chronology mixed up. The attack on Yugoslavia by the Germans preceded the creation of the NDH. The attack on Yugoslavia, as you indicated, began on April 7th, and it wasn't until several weeks later that the NDH was created, by which time the entire country had been conquered by German and Italian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: They did not bomb either Croatia or Slovenia, that's for sure, because Croatia was part of the Axis. Towards the end of the war, again Serbia alone was bombed, including Belgrade, Vranj, and other cities, and that was done by the Allied forces with the blessing of Marshal Tito?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That seems to be your testimony, but it is wrong. There were battles all over and bombarding of cities by German forces towards the end of the war in a number of different situations. So that's an extremely tendency and one-sided way of describing the end of the war in 1944/1945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have dealt with the First World War. We have the Second and the involvement of the Serbs in the two wars. You have raised the matter on which the witness differs from you. You're not going to settle. If it has to be settled, the Chamber will. You must now move to the 1990s. I think we have heard enough of the background, and I quite agree that you can't start with 1990, but I don't want to have any more on the First and Second World War. Move to the 1990s now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the camps in the NDH, isn't it true that hundreds of thousands of Serbs, Roma, and Jews were killed. Some sources say 700.000, other sources say 500.000, but in any case in the hundreds of thousands. Do you know anything of that? And with that I will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Tito regime immediately after the war spread the exactly myth that you just put forward; that, in fact, the number of the casualties in the Second World War was about two million and that the numbers of people who suffered in the camps, who died in the camps was in the many hundreds of thousands, and that number in the course of latter years of socialism has been challenged effectively by two very fine studies, showing the demographic losses owing to the Second World War; one by a Serb demographer and one by a Croat demographer. Those two studies both put the total number of war dead in the Second World War at about one million, considerably less than the Tito-era estimates, but nevertheless a strikingly large number of victims. They also examined the ethnicity of the casualties and found that in percentage terms, as percentage of the total population, the percentage of Serbs who died was very slightly greater than the percentage of Bosnian Muslims who died in the course of the war. I don't have those numbers right at my hand. I have written about those studies elsewhere, and would commend them to you for a very relatively reliable assessment of the human costs of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No more questions on this. Absolutely, no more. You will move to 1990 or end your cross-examination. We have had enough of the historical background, which concededly is of some significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will move directly to page 8, paragraph 2 in the English version; namely, the villages in Sarajevo. The villages with the Serbian majority were located to the east of Sarajevo in the mountainous area of Pale, in Ilijas, and other smaller settlements. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. Is that page 4 or page 8?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that's it, okay. Let me hurry up. So let's move to English page 9, paragraph 2, where you speak about the 1974 constitution, and you state there: "Six republics and two autonomous provinces received autonomy pursuant to the 1974 constitution; whereas, the presidents of the republics had very differing opinions as to how the federal state should be organised," and there you go on to say, "There were two camps, Separatist Nationalists and who were in principle Croats, Slovenes, and Kosovo Albanians; and on the other hand, Hegemonist Nationalists led by Slobodan Milosevic, President of the Republic of Serbia." Is that right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question relates to separatist and hegemonist. In 1974, when the constitution was passed, what did Slobodan Milosevic have to do with any of it, with the period when these concepts were embedded in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm describing here the dilemmas facing the newly elected officials of the city of Sarajevo; therefore, it applies to November, December 1990 and the period afterwards, by which time this divide between the hegemonists and separatists was substantial. And I have adopted the description in this very fine book by Raif Disdarovic, who tells of his time as President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia and experiencing frustration and disappointment with both camps in his effort to keep Yugoslavia together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, again, a politician from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did that constitution put the foundations in for the dissolution of Yugoslavia? Wasn't the SFRY crushed into its constituent republics as early as 1974?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think that is putting it too strongly, but I would agree that the seeds of this republicanisation were certainly embedded in the constitution of 1974 and became more pronounced after Tito's death in 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is the way it was envisaged, or rather Josip Broz Tito was elected a lifetime president. As soon as he died, the visions embedded in the 1974 constitution were supposed to be materialised. Is that not in fact what happened in 1988, or rather, 1981 when the -- with the demonstrations in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I your direction was to go to 1990, and we're now back to 1981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, 1990, Mr. Tapuskovic. That is in fact what the report is about, but I allowed you to deal with the background because I acknowledge there is a historical relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm referring to the direct causes of the horrors that happened in Yugoslavia. Look at the last sentence of the paragraph that deals with the federal system and the community. It says here: "The leaders of BiH found to be between a rock and a hard place because they appreciated being in Yugoslavia, but were afraid on the other hand that the Serb would go to dominate the rump Yugoslavia." Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll hurry up and skip ahead to the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the issue of military preparations or preparedness, you said on page 16, paragraph 3 -- that's actually paragraph 26 according to my numeration. The heading is "Military Preparations." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here you say, "In 1991 and earlier 1992 the three nationalists took measures to prepare militarily for war. Bosnian Muslim leaders of SDA sponsored the creation of two paramilitary groups; The Patriotic League and the Green Berets," and that's all you say here. Do you know that the Patriotic League and the Green Berets had been established back in the month of March 1991 as military units? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There were two meetings. One was indeed in March of 1991. The formal creation of the Patriotic League as a party instrument of the SDA was in, I believe, June 10th of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you read the books by their generals, the first Chief of the General Staff Sefer Halilovic and other authors? There were other generals who wrote books about this. Did you read such books? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's turn to Sefer Halilovic. I should like to read this out to you. I'm not sure if you speak Serbian/Croatian/Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It hasn't been translated. It's DD00-1636. I should like to read several passages to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, what are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the book by Sefer Halilovic, who was the first Chief of the General Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; therefore, man number one of the ABiH up until 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said you were going to read several passages. Just confine yourself to one or two, or three at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just two.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please state the page he is quoting from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the page? What is the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 7. I only took several pages from that book. That's page 7 at the bottom. I will read out just the first sentence: "Our forces were organised into the BiH Patriotic League in the units on the strengths of platoons, two detachments and brigades, numbering the total of 120.000 men." Page 9, it says: "I decided with the engagement of all the forces of," and he's talk become 1992. "I decide to use certain forces and to take in a quick action certain warehouses and facilities of the JNA, block barracks, prevent breaches and advances by the enemy, and as soon as favourable conditions are met to engage in extensive offensive activities with a view to crushing destroying and driving out the enemy from the BH territory." This was January 1992 when 120.000 men you were under arms. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: You've conversed these dates somewhat. We have agreed there was a meeting in March 1991, in with which the Patriotic League was formed in concept; and as I have indicated on June 10th 1991, a large convocation of SDA leaders the formed a Muslim, I believe it is called Muslim Council for National Defence. So the origins of these -- or for at least the Patriotic League go back to spring of 1991. You can also read in General Halilovic's book that there was very little activity, virtually nothing going on when he first appeared on scene in September of 1991, and was given the responsibility of leading the organising activities. I have indicated, certainly in my book, although I don't believe in this paper that by January of 1992 the Patriotic League was indeed effectively organised, was holding inspections, and was moving toward becoming more battle-ready, largely on the basis of a large number of volunteers, but with a great paucity of weaponry and ammunition. This in fact -- the citation that you have just read is a -- a standard part, but only one part, of the story of the preparation of the Patriotic League in the course of 1991, 1992, until the time of the outbreak of war in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to tender this document, DD00-1636, to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as D133.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm have no objection to object to it being admitted. I'm happy if it goes in. It doesn't need to be marked for identification. These are photocopied pages from the book by Sefer Halilovic. I had the benefit of Ms. Bosnjakovic beside me, and it slipped my mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So it's marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the same passage at the end of that passage, it says: "As stated above" -- I apologise. We're looking at the document based on which I am examining you, DD00-1462-52; English version page 16, paragraph 3, the penultimate sentence. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Can you just read a few words of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "The SDS, as described above, supported the JNA's Croatia campaign, coordinated plans with JNA units in BH." You're referring to the campaign against Croatia here, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA campaign against -- in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, when you were preparing this report, and I couldn't find this anywhere, did you have in mind the documents in possession of the Prosecution; namely, Presidency of the SFRY held on the 12th of July, 1991, starting at 10.30 and chaired by Stjepan Mesic. Did you ever see this document and go through it? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: You asked me two questions. One, did I base this conclusion on the that document and the answer is no. I don't know if I-- without out looking at it, if I have seen it. My source for this statements is -- there was a great deal of press coverage, particularly in the newspapers Glas and Kozarski Vjesnik, in the Bosnian Krajina dealing with the thousands of Bosnians who served in the JNA during the Croatian campaign, many of them having been essentially mobilised by the SDS at the initiative of Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, this wasn't my question. I wanted you to give me a yes or no answer to the following question: Whilst preparing your report, you did not use the SFRY Presidency record of the meeting held on the 12th of July at the time when Yugoslavia was still in existence, the meeting which dealt with the JNA and other topical issues. You did not take that report, or rather, that record into consideration, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I didn't use it in preparing this report, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You didn't use another document either; that's the minutes from the 189th meeting of the members of the SFRY Presidency, the extended Presidency held on the 2nd of March, 1992. You didn't use that one in preparing your report either?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, at least I think we're in the appropriate decade now, but, again, I renew my objection as to relevancy. We have yet to get to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not irrelevant, but remember the time constraints.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I may answer your question. Yes, I in fact did consult that document in the course of preparing this report. I didn't cite it, but I am aware of it and read through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, I should like to tender it as a Defence exhibit, DD00-1649. There is the English translation as well. I should like to read the main part of it, English page 2, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that document available in e-court at all Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I don't have a document under DD00-1469.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that on your list, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. That's DD00-1469. That was the number it was assigned. I have both the B/C/S and English versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just put the English version on the ELMO quickly. So what is the passage now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2 in the English version, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will read out only that one. The last paragraph on page 2. Can I proceed? Do you see that? This is the SFRY Presidency decision: "The SFRY Presidency emphasised that they would respect any political decision agreed upon by the three equal constituent nations living in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina could be prevented -- can be prevented if the international community followed such a diplomatic approach. "Therefore, the SFRY Presidency has called upon all the state and political structures as well as all three constituent nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina to take a reasonable and restrained approach in order to prevent an even greater tragedy that it would be difficult to contain." Did you take this into account in your report or when writing that sentence about the JNA launching a campaign against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The document of this -- or the date of this Presidency meeting? What is the date of this Presidency meeting? I'm not -- I understood it to be March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. One month before the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was mention of this matter that should be taken care of -- taken into account.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: By the time this session was held, the war in Croatia had begun and at least temporarily ended. And other than perhaps continuing the public posture of the JNA backed by the Presidency of playing this neutral role, which was only a small part of its actual role, I see no relevance between this document and the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to another subject now, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the English version, that's page 16, paragraph 4, where you speak of the wars in Slovenia and Croatia and how they started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, Your Honours, I would like to tender this document DD00-1649 into evidence. There is the translation of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, it's translated. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be D134.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 16, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There you refer to the wars in Slovenia and Croatia. You say that the Yugoslavia People's Army gradually transformed into a Serbian force. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that a conflict broke out in Slovenia and that the first war crimes were committed there when some 50 unarmeded soldiers were killed there when the barracks were surrounded, encircled? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't -- I can't confirm that, no. The war itself was, of course, a result of the Slovene declaration of independence and the subsequent JNA decision to seal off the -- to take control of the border crossing points from Slovenia into other countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: As soon as the JNA withdrew from Slovenia, all those who were JNA members and were Slovenes remained or stayed behind in the Slovenian army, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Nearly all of them did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the case in Croatia, too?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think the transformation of the JNA in Croatia took place during the course of the war, not so much at the time of the withdrawal. With hostilities beginning, many officers of Croat nationality and recruits of Croat nationality left the JNA, which was the reason that the JNA had to start mobilising recruits in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I would just place that development to well advance -- in advance of the actual withdrawal which only began in January of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Talking about Croatia, do you know Tudjman's -- Tudjman's well-known sentence in these courtrooms, saying, "There would have been no war if we hadn't wanted it?"

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I really have to rise on relevance with respect to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you demonstrate the relevance, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was no Croatia campaign and what the Presidency of Yugoslavia had foreseen on the 12th of July did happen in Slovenia, did happen in Croatia and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer. We rule it irrelevant. Move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And next paragraph, English page 17, paragraph 2 you speak of the Territorial Defence. Is that true? And you say here that: "Units of the Territorial Defence were organised at the local level, primarily in factories, offices, and other places of work." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you continue: "Since TO units were designed to operate even in the absence of the JNA and in the event of an invasion." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of invasion was to be expected in 1974 in Yugoslavia? An invasion by who? And wasn't that -- here's my question, or rather I'll drop this one. Territorial Defence was established under the terms of the 1974 constitution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I believe it predated the 1974 constitution. The entire defence theory and organisation was restructured in the time after the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the theory of the armed people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did all those Territorial Defences, once the war had started, because that's how they had been designed, so once the civil war started, did they not turn the armies of the respective republics, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina ones -- the one -- some units sided with the Serbs, others with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In Croatia the core of the Croatian army was really the Ministry of Defence -- or of Ministry of the Interior, not the Territorial Defence. In Bosnia, the Territorial Defence, Bosnian central command became the, in a sense, the top command of the military forces that eventually became the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I must hurry. Just a moment, I'm referring to page -- no, I must hurry; therefore, I will skip all this that refers to the beginning of the war, and I'll come immediately to the siege upon which my learned friend insists. And that's on page 51 A -- or rather, 29, page 29 in the English version, the last paragraph. It's a lengthy paragraph mentioning Ratko Mladic. Perhaps I can squeeze this in if other things do not fit in anymore. You mention Ratko Mladic, and I would like to read it out as a whole. Have you found it? I will read it out very slowly. The diplomacy advocated by Mladic became an essential part of the dual track approach to the siege adopted by Serbian leaders. No inverted comas here. The public position of senior SDS officials and of senior commanders of the VRS was that Serb Armed Forces were merely defending the Serb inhabited areas around Sarajevo against assaults by the ABiH." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I wrote here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you go on to say: "Bosnian Serb leaders resolutely declined to call the military situation 'a siege,' the term normally used by global media and US and UN officials. Instead Mladic claimed that Bosnian Muslim forces were attacking Serbs in Sarajevo's suburbs from within the city and holding Serbs in the city centre against their will. The Serb side was and still is deeply disturbed by the situation that now prevails in Sarajevo, he wrote in an open letter to UN Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali and several western leaders in September 1992." And it continues: "Between 40.000 to 50.000 Serbs are held as ethnic hostages and the constant daily attacks on Serbian municipalities Ilidza, Lukavica, Ilijas, Vogosca take place. He accounted for civilian casualties in the city by blaming the city's defenders." The Muslim side keeps committing crimes against their own population, bombing their own cities and towns, killing their own people in bread queues, on marketplaces, at funerals, attacking UNPROFOR, United Nations Protection Force personnel and facilities and now starting to shoot down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask a question now. What's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is: What the witness knows, what the situation was like between August 1994 and November 1995. Are you familiar with the fact that there was a tunnel, apart from everything else, and what the situation was like on the battlefield. Do you know anything about this time-period, given the fact that my learned friend insists so much on the siege.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the city in January of 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you're familiar with the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Next question, Mr. -- he's familiar with it. What's the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 34, the last paragraph, if you have found it. It refers to the visit of Tadeusz Masowiecki, who was a human rights officer, and he speaks of the terror among the Sarajevo residents. Do you know how many Serbs were killed in 1992 in Sarajevo and that according to some -- to recent information the number of persons killed thus is several thousand. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That is not a supportable number of Serb deaths in 1992. In fact, the number of Serbs who died in 1992 is the subject of a couple of ongoing investigations. One estimate by a demographer who has attempted to enumerate all the deaths in Bosnia-Herzegovina came up with the number 151 Serbs killed in encounters with Croat or Bosnian Muslim irregulars within the city, but the number of Serbs killed by the artillery fire and sniping and tank fire from the hills is obviously much greater than that. The highest possible number of Serbs that were killed in that period was attempted to be provided by the government of the Republika Srpska in a report in 2005, and they enumerated 2.511 individuals. That report, however, as it was investigated by various news reporters turned out to include people who been killed, Serbs who had killed in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbs who had died from the shelling and sniping, and furthermore --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: -- at least one person who is still alive. So that number is unquestionably high.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. That wasn't my question. Tadeusz Masowiecki came to Bosnia and submitted a report about the camps. So you don't know anything about the camps in Sarajevo that outnumber 100 in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995 where people were being killed and thrown into tanks or containers. So you don't know that the people in Sarajevo were subject to the fiercest terror, or do you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
